docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The arrival rate \(\lambda\) of a Poisson process is the average number of arrivals per unit time. In a time interval of length \(t\), the expected number of arrivals is \(\lambda t\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The rate parameter controls the time scale. A larger \(\lambda\) means arrivals are more frequent, so waiting times are shorter. In the exponential waiting-time distribution associated with a Poisson process, the mean waiting time is \(1/\lambda\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(N_t\) is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\), then \(E[N_t]=\lambda t\).
  • The first waiting time \(T_1\) satisfies \(T_1\sim\operatorname{Expo}(\lambda)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If calls arrive at rate \(3\) per hour, the expected number of calls in \(2\) hours is \(6\).
  • If radioactive decay is modeled with rate \(\lambda\), the half-life is \(\log(2)/\lambda\).

docs.title: Axiom
docs.text:
A probability function \(P\) on a sample space \(S\) satisfies the axioms of probability if:

  1. \(P(A)\ge 0\) for every event \(A\).
  2. \(P(S)=1\).
  3. If \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) are pairwise disjoint events, then
\[ P\left(\bigcup_{i=1}^{\infty} A_i\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{\infty}P(A_i). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The axioms say that probabilities are non-negative, total certainty has probability one, and mutually exclusive alternatives add. Almost all calculation rules in elementary probability follow from these three statements, so they replace intuition by a precise mathematical structure.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(P(\emptyset)=0\) follows by applying countable additivity to repeated empty events.
  • If \(A\subseteq B\), then \(P(A)\le P(B)\).
  • \(P(A^c)=1-P(A)\) for every event \(A\).
  • For two events, \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Naive probability satisfies the axioms when the sample space is finite and equally likely.
  • A model with events \(A_i\) having probabilities \(2^{-i}\) for \(i=1,2,\ldots\) can be valid even though the sample space is infinite.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with positive probabilities, Bayes' rule is

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A)P(A)}{P(B)}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Bayes' rule reverses the direction of conditioning. It combines a prior probability \(P(A)\) with the likelihood \(P(B\mid A)\) and then normalizes by the total probability of observing \(B\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• With a partition \(A_1,\ldots,A_n\), Bayes' rule becomes \(P(A_i\mid B)=\frac{P(B\mid A_i)P(A_i)}{\sum_j P(B\mid A_j)P(A_j)}\).
  • Bayes' rule explains why base rates matter in testing and classification problems.
  • It is a direct consequence of the definition of conditional probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In a medical-test problem, sensitivity and specificity describe probabilities of test results conditional on disease status; Bayes rule converts them into the probability of disease given a positive test.
  • If \(K\) is the event that a student knows an answer and \(R\) is the event that the response is correct, Bayes rule computes \(P(K\mid R)\) from \(P(R\mid K)\), \(P(R\mid K^c)\), and \(P(K)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has a Bernoulli distribution with parameter \(p\in[0,1]\) if

\[ P(X=1)=p,\qquad P(X=0)=1-p. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Bernoulli distribution models one yes/no trial, success/failure trial, or indicator of an event. It is the building block for the binomial and geometric distributions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=p\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=p(1-p)\).
  • If \(A\) is an event, then \(I_A\sim\operatorname{Bern}(P(A))\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair coin head indicator is Bernoulli\((1/2)\).
  • The indicator of the event “a die roll is six” is Bernoulli\((1/6)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\), read “\(n\) choose \(k\)”, is

\[ \binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!} \]

for integers \(0\le k\le n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: It counts how many size-\(k\) subsets can be chosen from an \(n\)-element set. The denominator removes the orderings inside the selected group and the unselected group.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Symmetry: \(\binom{n}{k}=\binom{n}{n-k}\).
  • Story-proof identities arise when the same counting problem is solved in two different ways, such as choosing a team and then a captain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) because the two-object selections from \(\{A,B,C\}\) are \(\{A,B\}\), \(\{A,C\}\), and \(\{B,C\}\).
  • The number of ways to form a five-card hand is \(\binom{52}{5}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has a binomial distribution with parameters \(n\) and \(p\) if

\[ P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k},\qquad k=0,1,\ldots,n. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A binomial random variable counts the number of successes in \(n\) independent Bernoulli trials with the same success probability \(p\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=np\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=np(1-p)\).
  • If \(X_i\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) are independent, then \(\sum_{i=1}^n X_i\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of heads in ten independent tosses of a coin with head probability \(p\) is \(\operatorname{Bin}(10,p)\).
  • If two independent groups count successes with the same success probability, their total count is binomial with the combined number of trials.

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The birthday problem asks for the probability that at least two draws from a finite set produce the same value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: It is usually easier to count the complement: no repeated value. This turns a difficult “at least one match” event into an ordered no-collision count.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(n\) draws are made uniformly with replacement from \(m\) possible values, then the probability of at least one match is
\[ 1-\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}, \qquad n\le m. \]
  • The method applies far beyond birthdays: survey IDs, hash collisions, and repeated sampled labels use the same structure.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For birthdays with \(m=365\), the complement is that all birthdays are different.
  • If 1000 respondents are sampled from \(10^6\) possible IDs with replacement, the event that someone is chosen more than once can be computed by subtracting the no-repeat probability from \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu=E[X]\), the \(n\)th central moment is

\[ E[(X-\mu)^n], \]

provided the expectation exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Central moments measure powers of deviations from the mean. Centering removes the location of the distribution and focuses on spread or shape around the mean. The second central moment is the variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The second central moment is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=E[(X-\mu)^2]\).
  • The third and fourth central moments are used in standardized form to define skewness and kurtosis.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is constant with probability one, then every positive central moment is \(0\).
  • If \(X\) is symmetric about its mean and the third central moment exists, then \(E[(X-\mu)^3]=0\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(Z\) has mean \(a\) and variance \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)\), then for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ P(|Z-a|\ge\varepsilon)\le \frac{E[(Z-a)^2]}{\varepsilon^2}. \]

In particular, when \(a=E[Z]\),

\[ P(|Z-E[Z]|\ge\varepsilon)\le \frac{\operatorname{Var}(Z)}{\varepsilon^2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Chebyshev's inequality gives a distribution-free bound on the probability of being far from the mean. It is often not sharp, but it requires only a finite variance.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Equivalently, \(P(|X-\mu|\ge k\sigma)\le 1/k^2\) for \(k>0\).
  • Chebyshev's inequality is a standard route to proving the weak law of large numbers for independent variables with common finite variance.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\operatorname{Var}(Z)=4\), then \(P(|Z-E[Z]|\ge10)\le4/100=0.04\).
  • For a sample mean with variance \(\sigma^2/n\), doubling \(n\) halves the Chebyshev upper bound for a fixed \(\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A combination is an unordered selection of objects from a larger collection.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Use combinations when only the selected group matters, not the order in which the objects were chosen. A hand of cards is usually a combination because drawing ace-then-king and king-then-ace produces the same hand.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of ways to choose \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects is the binomial coefficient \(\binom{n}{k}\).
  • Combinations remove the \(k!\) overcount that appears when an unordered group is first counted as an ordered list.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Choosing 2 apples from 3 different apples gives \(\binom{3}{2}=3\) possible selections.
  • A five-card hand from a 52-card deck gives \(\binom{52}{5}\) possible hands.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The complement of an event \(A\), written \(A^c\), is the set of all outcomes in the sample space that are not in \(A\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The complement is the event that \(A\) does not occur. It is especially useful when the desired event is difficult to count directly but its opposite is easy to count.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(P(A^c)=1-P(A)\).
  • \(A\cup A^c=S\) and \(A\cap A^c=\emptyset\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one die roll, if \(A=\{6\}\), then \(A^c=\{1,2,3,4,5\}\) and \(P(A^c)=5/6\).
  • In birthday-type problems, it is often easier to compute the probability of no match first and then subtract from \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the elementary event-based setting, the conditional expectation \(E(Y\mid X=x)\) is the expectation of \(Y\) computed under the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conditional expectation is an average after information has been revealed. It answers: if we know that the conditioning event or value occurred, what is the expected value now? For example, the conditional distribution of \(Y\) changes depending on whether \(X=0\) or \(X=1\), so the conditional expectation changes as well.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X=0\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\), then \(E(Y\mid X=0)=1\).
  • If \(Y\mid X=1\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\), then \(E(Y\mid X=1)=3\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a machine is in state \(X=0\), the number of arrivals may have one Poisson mean; if it is in state \(X=1\), it may have another.
  • If a test result is known, the expected loss or payoff after observing the result can differ from the unconditional expectation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Events \(A\) and \(B\) are conditionally independent given \(C\) if \(P(C)>0\) and

\[ P(A\cap B\mid C)=P(A\mid C)P(B\mid C). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conditional independence means that after restricting attention to the information \(C\), knowing \(A\) gives no further information about \(B\). It is independence inside a conditional probability model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conditional independence does not necessarily imply unconditional independence.
  • Unconditional independence does not necessarily imply conditional independence after adding new information.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Two coin-toss events can be independent before conditioning, but become dependent after conditioning on an event such as “exactly one head occurred”.
  • In diagnostic reasoning, symptoms may be conditionally independent given a disease state even if they are not independent overall.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For events \(A\) and \(B\) with \(P(B)>0\), the conditional probability of \(A\) given \(B\) is

\[ P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conditioning means that \(B\) is treated as the new information set. Inside that reduced situation, \(P(A\mid B)\) measures the fraction of the probability mass of \(B\) that also lies in \(A\). This is why conditioning changes probabilities: the denominator is no longer the whole sample space but the event known to have occurred.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For fixed \(B\) with \(P(B)>0\), \(P(\cdot\mid B)\) satisfies the axioms of probability.
  • The multiplication rule follows: \(P(A\cap B)=P(A\mid B)P(B)\).
  • In general \(P(A\mid B)\ne P(B\mid A)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a selected card is known to be red, the probability that it is a heart is \(1/2\).
  • In a multiple-choice question, the probability a student knew the answer given that the answer is correct is not the same as the probability of a correct answer given that the student knew it.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The conditional variance \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=x)\) is the variance of \(Y\) computed under the conditional distribution of \(Y\) given \(X=x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Conditional variance measures spread after conditioning on known information. The distribution of \(Y\) can become more or less variable depending on the value of the conditioning variable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For a Poisson conditional distribution, the conditional variance equals the conditional mean.
  • Conditional variance is not the same object as unconditional variance; mixing over different conditions can add extra variability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\mid X=0\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=0)=1\).
  • If \(Y\mid X=1\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X=1)=3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A continuous random variable is a random variable whose distribution can be described by a probability density function.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuous random variable spreads probability over intervals rather than assigning positive probability to individual points. In models such as \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) or \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), probabilities are areas under a density curve. Therefore \(P(X=a)=0\) for a single fixed value \(a\), even though intervals containing \(a\) can have positive probability.

This is why endpoint choices usually do not matter for continuous distributions: \((0,1)\), \([0,1)\), and \([0,1]\) lead to the same uniform probabilities when they differ only at individual points.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For any \(a<b\), \(P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)=\int_a^b f_X(t)\,dt\).
  • A density is not itself a probability; it becomes a probability only after integration over an interval.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(P(0.2<U<0.7)=0.5\) because the interval has length \(0.5\).
  • If \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), then \(P(0.7<Z\le 1.7)=\Phi(1.7)-\Phi(0.7)\), where \(\Phi\) is the standard normal CDF.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A sequence of random variables \(X_n\) converges in probability to a number \(a\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\),

\[ P(|X_n-a|\ge\varepsilon)\to0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Convergence in probability means that large deviations from the target become unlikely. It does not require every realized sequence to move smoothly toward the target; it says the probability of being outside any fixed tolerance band goes to zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(E[X_n]=a\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X_n)\to0\), then \(X_n\to a\) in probability by Chebyshev's inequality.
  • The sample mean of i.i.d. variables with finite variance converges in probability to the population mean.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\bar X_n\) has mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2/n\), then \(P(|\bar X_n-\mu|\ge\varepsilon)\le \sigma^2/(n\varepsilon^2)\).
  • A histogram bin height, written as an average of indicators, converges in probability to the bin probability.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Counting is the process of determining the number of outcomes in a finite set or event, usually without listing every outcome explicitly.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: In probability, counting answers two questions: how large is the sample space, and how large is the event of interest? The right method depends on whether order matters, whether repetition is allowed, and whether the objects being counted are distinguishable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Ordered multi-step choices are usually counted by the multiplication rule.
  • Unordered selections are often counted with a combination; unordered selections with repetition are counted with stars and bars.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Rolling a six-sided die five times gives \(6^5\) ordered outcomes because each roll has six possibilities.
  • Drawing a five-card hand from a standard deck gives \(\binom{52}{5}\) hands because order is ignored.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The cumulative distribution function of a random variable \(X\) is

\[ F_X(x)=P(X\le x),\qquad x\in\mathbb{R}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The CDF accumulates all probability up to a threshold \(x\). It works for discrete, continuous, and mixed distributions, so it is often the most general way to describe a one-dimensional distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every CDF is non-decreasing and right-continuous.
  • \(\lim_{x\to-\infty}F_X(x)=0\) and \(\lim_{x\to\infty}F_X(x)=1\).
  • For any \(a<b\), \(P(a<X\le b)=F_X(b)-F_X(a)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die roll \(X\), \(F_X(3)=P(X\le 3)=1/2\).
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), the CDF is \(0\) below \(0\), jumps to \(1/2\) on \([0,1)\), and jumps to \(1\) at \(1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable has a degenerate distribution at \(a\) if

\[ P(X=a)=1. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A degenerate random variable is random in notation but not in outcome: it equals the same constant with probability one. Degenerate distributions appear naturally as limits, for example when a sample mean becomes more and more concentrated around the population mean.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(P(X=a)=1\), then \(E[X]=a\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=0\).
  • Conversely, if a variance exists and equals \(0\), then the random variable is constant with probability one.
  • A degenerate distribution has all probability concentrated at a single point.
  • Its variance is zero.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A random variable that always pays exactly \(5\) has a degenerate distribution at \(5\).
  • As \(n\) grows, the sample mean of i.i.d. variables with finite variance converges in probability to a degenerate limit at \(\mu\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A discrete random variable is a random variable \(X\) for which there is a finite or countably infinite set \(C\) such that \(P(X\in C)=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Discrete random variables have values that can be listed: \(x_1,x_2,\ldots\). The list may be finite, like the number of heads in ten coin tosses, or infinite, like the number of failures before the first success in repeated Bernoulli trials. The key point is that probability is assigned to individual possible values through a PMF.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A discrete random variable is described by its probability mass function \(p_X(x)=P(X=x)\).
  • The probabilities of all possible values add to one: \(\sum_{x\in\operatorname{supp}(X)}p_X(x)=1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of heads in ten coin tosses is discrete with possible values \(0,1,\ldots,10\).
  • A Poisson random variable is discrete with possible values \(0,1,2,\ldots\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has the discrete uniform distribution on a finite set \(C\) with \(n\) elements, written \(X\sim\operatorname{Dunif}(C)\), if

\[ P(X=x)=\frac1n \quad \text{for each }x\in C. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Discrete uniform means every listed value is equally likely. It is the probability model behind fair dice, equally likely cards when modelled correctly, and finite random choices.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The PMF is constant on the support and zero outside it.
  • If all support points are equally likely, every support point is a mode.
  • All points in the finite support have the same probability.
  • Naive probability is exactly discrete uniform probability on the chosen sample space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair six-sided die roll has the discrete uniform distribution on \(\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}\).
  • A random variable uniformly distributed on \(\{1,2,\ldots,n\}\) has mean \((n+1)/2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint if \(A\cap B=\emptyset\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Disjoint events cannot occur together. This is different from independence: if two non-empty events are disjoint, learning that one occurred makes the other impossible.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, then \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\).
  • If \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) are pairwise disjoint, countable additivity gives \(P(\bigcup_i A_i)=\sum_i P(A_i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In one die roll, “roll a 1” and “roll a 6” are disjoint.
  • In a single chess game, “win”, “draw”, and “loss” are disjoint outcomes.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The distribution of a random variable describes how probability is allocated over its possible values.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The distribution is the complete probability description of \(X\). Two random variables may be different functions, may live on different sample spaces, or may be dependent on each other, while still having the same distribution. What matters for equality in distribution is that they assign the same probabilities to the same numerical events.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The CDF \(F_X(x)=P(X\le x)\) uniquely determines the distribution of a real-valued random variable.
  • For a discrete random variable, the PMF determines the CDF and therefore the full distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_1\) is the first coin toss indicator and \(Y_1=1-X_1\) for a fair coin, then \(X_1\) and \(Y_1\) have the same Bernoulli distribution, even though they are perfectly dependent.
  • A variable \(Y\) chosen as \(X_1\) with probability \(p\) and \(X_2\) with probability \(1-p\) has a mixture distribution with CDF \(pF_1+(1-p)F_2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An event is a subset of the sample space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An event is a statement about the outcome, represented as the set of outcomes for which that statement is true. After the experiment is performed, the event occurs exactly when the realized outcome belongs to that set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The empty set \(\emptyset\) is the impossible event.
  • The sample space \(S\) is the certain event.
  • Set operations on events represent logical operations: union means ‘or’, intersection means ‘and’, complement means ‘not’.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If one fair die is rolled, the event “an even number is rolled” is \(A=\{2,4,6\}\).
  • If two coins are tossed, the event “exactly one head occurs” is \(B=\{HT,TH\}\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random variable \(X\) with PMF \(p_X\), the expectation or expected value is

$$ E[X]=\sum_x x\,p_X(x), $$ provided the sum exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Expectation is a probability-weighted average. It is a long-run average interpretation when repeated identical trials make sense, but it does not have to be a value that the random variable can actually take.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If two random variables have the same distribution and the expectation exists, they have the same expectation.
  • Linearity: \(E[aX+bY]=aE[X]+bE[Y]\) whenever the expectations exist.
  • For nonnegative integer-valued \(X\), \(E[X]=\sum_{k\ge1}P(X\ge k)\) when the sum is finite or infinite in the extended sense.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), then \(E(X)=p\).
  • If \(X\) is the payoff of €100 for heads and €0 for tails with a fair coin, then \(E(X)=50\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has an exponential distribution with rate \(\lambda>0\) if

\[ f_X(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x},\qquad x\ge0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The exponential distribution models waiting times between arrivals in a Poisson process. The rate \(\lambda\) is the average number of arrivals per unit time, so larger \(\lambda\) means shorter waiting times.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=1/\lambda\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=1/\lambda^2\).
  • Memorylessness: \(P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(T\) is the time to radioactive decay and \(T\sim\operatorname{Expo}(\lambda)\), then the half-life solves \(P(T>t)=1/2\), giving \(t=\log(2)/\lambda\).
  • If offers above a threshold arrive through an exponential tail, the excess above the threshold has the same exponential form by memorylessness.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a natural number \(n\), the factorial \(n!\) is

\[ n! = n(n-1)(n-2)\cdots 1, \]

with the convention \(0!=1\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The factorial counts how many ways \(n\) distinct objects can be put into a complete order. The convention \(0!=1\) makes counting formulas work cleanly when no objects are selected or no positions remain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• There are \(n!\) permutations of \(n\) distinct objects.
  • Factorials appear in binomial coefficients: \(\binom{n}{k}=\frac{n!}{k!(n-k)!}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Three different apples can be assigned to three ordered people in \(3!=6\) ways.
  • A full ordering of 52 distinct cards has \(52!\) possible orders.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A folded normal distribution is the distribution of \(Y=|X|\) when \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Taking an absolute value folds all negative values of a normal variable onto the positive half-line. This transformation changes the shape of the distribution because probability mass from both \(x=y\) and \(x=-y\) contributes to the density at \(y>0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(y\ge0\), \(F_Y(y)=P(|X|\le y)=\Phi((y-\mu)/\sigma)-\Phi((-y-\mu)/\sigma)\).
  • For \(y>0\), a density is \(f_Y(y)=\frac1\sigma\varphi((y-\mu)/\sigma)+\frac1\sigma\varphi((y+\mu)/\sigma)\).
  • A folded normal random variable is the absolute value of a normal random variable.
  • It appears when only magnitude is observed and the sign is discarded.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim N(0,1)\), then \(|X|\) measures the distance of \(X\) from zero and is always nonnegative.
  • If \(\mu\ne0\), the two terms in the density reflect contributions from the right and left sides of the original normal curve.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: If \(X\) is a random variable and \(g:\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is a function, then \(g(X)\) is the random variable defined by \(g(X)(s)=g(X(s))\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function of a random variable is another random variable. The original distribution of \(X\) determines the distribution of \(g(X)\), but the transformation can merge values, stretch values, shift values, or change the shape of the distribution.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• To find the distribution of \(g(X)\), describe events such as \(\{g(X)\le y\}\) in terms of \(X\).
  • To find \(E(g(X))\), LOTUS often avoids the extra step of first deriving the full distribution of \(g(X)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is a die roll and \(g(x)=x^2\), then \(g(X)\) is the square of the die roll.
  • If \(X\) has distribution function \(F\), then \(F(X)\) is a transformed random variable; in continuous strictly increasing cases it is uniform on \((0,1)\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For any event \(A\) with indicator random variable \(I_A\),

\[ E(I_A)=P(A). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The fundamental bridge turns a probability problem into an expectation problem. Because indicators only take the values \(0\) and \(1\), their average is exactly the probability of seeing a \(1\), i.e. the probability that the event occurs.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Inclusion-exclusion follows by taking expectations of indicator identities.
  • Probability bounds can be obtained by comparing an indicator to a nonnegative random variable and then using monotonicity of expectation.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A\) is “the die roll is six,” then \(I_A\) has expectation \(1/6\).
  • Since \(I_{A\cup B}=I_A+I_B-I_AI_B\), taking expectations gives \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A generated event of a random variable \(X:S\to\mathbb{R}\) is an event of the form \(\{X\in C\}\) for some set \(C\subseteq\mathbb{R}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The expression \(\{X\in C\}\) is shorthand for all outcomes whose \(X\)-value lies in \(C\). It is not a set of numbers; it is a subset of the original sample space. This distinction is important because probabilities are assigned to events in the sample space, while \(C\) is only the numerical condition used to select those outcomes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\{X=x\}\) means \(X^{-1}(\{x\})\), the set of outcomes mapped to \(x\).
  • \(\{X\le x\}\) is the event used to define the CDF \(F_X(x)=P(X\le x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\) is the number of heads in ten tosses, then \(\{X=0\}\) is the one event where all tosses are tails.
  • If \(X\) is a die roll, then \(\{X\in\{2,4,6\}\}\) is the event that the die roll is even.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In this course convention, a random variable \(X\) has the geometric distribution with parameter \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{Geom}(p)\), if it counts the number of failures before the first success in independent Bernoulli trials:

\[ P(X=n)=p(1-p)^n, \qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The geometric distribution is the one-success version of the negative binomial distribution. It models waiting in discrete trials. Be careful with conventions: some texts count the trial number of the first success instead of the number of failures before it.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Under this convention, \(E(X)=(1-p)/p\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=(1-p)/p^2\).
  • The geometric distribution has a discrete memoryless property.
  • The geometric distribution is memoryless on the nonnegative or positive integer scale, depending on convention.
  • It is the waiting-time distribution for repeated independent Bernoulli trials.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a coin has head probability \(p\), the number of tails before the first head is geometric.
  • If each offer is acceptable with probability \(p\), the number of rejected offers before the first acceptable one is geometric.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an exponential lifetime \(T\sim\operatorname{Expo}(\lambda)\), the half-life is the time \(t_{1/2}\) such that

\[ P(T>t_{1/2})=\frac12. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The half-life is the time by which the survival probability has fallen to one half. For exponential lifetimes, it is also the median lifetime. It depends inversely on the rate: higher rate means shorter half-life.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Since \(P(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}\), the half-life is \(t_{1/2}=\log(2)/\lambda\).
  • The half-life is not the same as the mean lifetime \(1/\lambda\), though both decrease as \(\lambda\) increases.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(\lambda=0.1\), then \(t_{1/2}=\log(2)/0.1\approx6.93\) time units.
  • If the rate doubles, the half-life is cut in half.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A histogram divides observed data into consecutive, non-overlapping bins and displays the frequency or relative frequency of observations in each bin.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A histogram is an empirical picture of a distribution. With relative frequencies, the height of a bin estimates the probability that an observation falls in that interval. With suitable rescaling by bin width, the histogram can approximate a probability density function.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(h_i=\frac1n\sum_{j=1}^n I_{\{X_j\in[b_i,b_{i+1})\}}\), then \(h_i\) is a sample mean of indicator variables.
  • For i.i.d. observations, \(h_i\) converges in probability to \(P(X\in[b_i,b_{i+1}))=F(b_{i+1})-F(b_i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Repeated coin-toss sample proportions form histograms that concentrate around the true success probability as the number of tosses grows.
  • If \(F\) is differentiable and the bin is narrow, then \(F(b_{i+1})-F(b_i)\approx f(c_i)(b_{i+1}-b_i)\) for some point \(c_i\) in the bin.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The hypergeometric distribution models the number \(X\) of white objects drawn when \(n\) objects are sampled without replacement from a population with \(w\) white and \(b\) black objects:

\[ P(X=k)=\frac{\binom{w}{k}\binom{b}{n-k}}{\binom{w+b}{n}}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is the finite-population analogue of a binomial count. The key difference is that sampling is without replacement, so the draws are dependent. The formula counts favourable samples divided by all samples.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The possible values satisfy \(\max\{0,n-b\}\le k\le\min\{n,w\}\).
  • For large populations with small sampling fractions, the hypergeometric distribution is often close to a binomial distribution.
  • It models sampling without replacement from a finite population.
  • Unlike the binomial distribution, draws are dependent because the population composition changes after each draw.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Drawing cards from a deck without replacement gives hypergeometric counts for suits or ranks.
  • Sampling \(n\) products from a batch with \(w\) defective products gives a hypergeometric count of defectives.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Random variables \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed if they have the same distribution, equivalently if \(P(X\le x)=P(Y\le x)\) for every real number \(x\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Identically distributed does not mean equal. It only means that the two random variables have the same probability pattern over numerical values. They can still be dependent, and they can even be functions of the same outcome.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If two random variables have the same CDF, then they have the same distribution.
  • If \(X\) and \(Y\) are identically distributed and their expectations exist, then \(E(X)=E(Y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For one fair coin toss, \(X\) equal to the head indicator and \(1-X\) are identically distributed Bernoulli\((1/2)\) variables, but they are not independent.
  • Two different fair coin toss indicators are both Bernoulli\((1/2)\) and, if the tosses are independent, also independent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. if they are independent random variables and all have the same distribution.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The phrase i.i.d. combines two different assumptions. “Independent” says the observations do not influence each other. “Identically distributed” says they are generated by the same probability law. This is the standard model for repeated measurements under unchanged conditions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\), then the sample mean has expectation \(\mu\).
  • If they also have variance \(\sigma^2\), then the sample mean has variance \(\sigma^2/n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Repeated independent tosses of the same coin give i.i.d. Bernoulli random variables.
  • Independent waiting times drawn from the same exponential distribution are i.i.d. exponential random variables.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The inclusion-exclusion principle computes the probability of a union by adding individual probabilities and subtracting overlaps that have been counted too many times.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: When \(P(A)+P(B)\) is formed, outcomes in \(A\cap B\) are counted twice. Subtracting the intersection once corrects the overcount.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two events,
\[ P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B). \]
  • For three events, add the single-event probabilities, subtract all pairwise intersections, then add the triple intersection.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(P(A)=0.4\), \(P(B)=0.3\), and \(P(A\cap B)=0.1\), then \(P(A\cup B)=0.6\).
  • If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint, the formula reduces to \(P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Two events \(A\) and \(B\) are independent if

\[ P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Independence means that learning one event occurred does not change the probability of the other. It does not mean that the events are disjoint.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A\) and \(B\) are disjoint and both have positive probability, then they are not independent.
  • Mutual independence for many events is stronger than pairwise independence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In two fair coin tosses, “first toss is heads” and “second toss is tails” are independent.
  • In seven independent chess games with equally likely win/draw/loss results, the probability of seven draws is \((1/3)^7\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Random variables are independent if events generated by them are independent. For two real-valued random variables \(X\) and \(Y\), this means that events such as \(\{X\in A\}\) and \(\{Y\in B\}\) are independent for all appropriate numerical sets \(A\) and \(B\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Independence is about information. Knowing the value of one independent random variable does not change the distribution of the other. Identical distributions and independence are separate ideas: variables can have the same distribution but be dependent, or have different distributions but be independent.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent and the expectations exist, then \(E(XY)=E(X)E(Y)\).
  • If \(X\) and \(Y\) are independent and have finite variances, then \(\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The head indicators of two independent coin tosses are independent Bernoulli random variables.
  • If \(X_1\) is a fair coin indicator and \(Y_1=1-X_1\), then \(X_1\) and \(Y_1\) have the same distribution but are dependent.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For an event \(A\), the indicator random variable \(I_A\) is defined by

\[ I_A(s)=\begin{cases}1,&s\in A,\\0,&s\notin A.\end{cases} \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: An indicator converts an event into a numerical random variable. It equals one when the event occurs and zero otherwise. This small conversion is powerful because it lets probability questions be handled using expectation.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E(I_A)=P(A)\).
  • Indicator algebra mirrors event algebra: \(I_{A\cap B}=I_AI_B\) and \(I_{A\cup B}=I_A+I_B-I_AI_B\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(A\) is “a die roll is even,” then \(I_A\) is \(1\) for rolls \(2,4,6\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  • If \(X_i\) is the indicator of a head on toss \(i\), then \(X_1+\cdots+X_n\) counts the number of heads.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If \(B_1,\ldots,B_n\) is a partition of the sample space with \(P(B_i)>0\), then for every event \(A\) the law of total probability states that

\[ P(A)=\sum_{i=1}^n P(A\mid B_i)P(B_i). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The law breaks a probability into cases. Compute the probability of \(B\) in each case, then average those conditional probabilities using the probabilities of the cases.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For two cases, \(P(B)=P(B\mid A)P(A)+P(B\mid A^c)P(A^c)\).
  • Bayes rule often uses the law of total probability to expand the denominator \(P(B)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A test-positive probability can be split into infected and not infected cases.
  • A message-transmission problem can be split according to the path or intermediate signal through which the message travels.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If the expectations exist, then for random variables \(X,Y\) and constants \(a,b\),

\[ E(aX+bY)=aE(X)+bE(Y). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Linearity is one of the most useful facts about expectation because it does not require independence. Even when random variables are dependent, the expected value of a sum is the sum of expected values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E(X_1+\cdots+X_n)=E(X_1)+\cdots+E(X_n)\) whenever the expectations exist.
  • \(E(cX)=cE(X)\) and \(E(a+X)=a+E(X)\) for constants \(a,c\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_1,X_2\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), then \(E(X_1+X_2)=2p\), independent or not.
  • The expected number of heads in \(n\) coin tosses is the sum of the expectations of the \(n\) head indicators.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A positive random variable \(Y\) has a lognormal distribution if \(Y=e^X\) for some normally distributed random variable \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A lognormal variable is obtained by exponentiating a normal variable. It is always positive and typically right-skewed. The exponentiation changes the relationship between mean, median, and mode: they are no longer all the same as in the underlying normal scale.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The median of \(Y=e^X\) is \(e^\mu\).
  • The mode of \(Y=e^X\) is \(e^{\mu-\sigma^2}\), which is less than \(e^\mu\) when \(\sigma>0\).
  • If \(Y\) is normal, then \(X=e^Y\) is lognormal.
  • A lognormal random variable is positive and often right-skewed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim N(0,1)\) and \(Y=e^X\), then the median of \(Y\) is \(1\).
  • Saying that the mode of \(Y=e^X\) is \(\mu\) is a category error: \(Y\) is positive, while \(\mu\) may be any real number.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
For a discrete random variable \(X\) and a function \(g\), the law of the unconscious statistician says

\[ E(g(X))=\sum_x g(x)P(X=x), \]

whenever the expectation is well-defined.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: LOTUS says that to average a transformed random variable \(g(X)\), you can use the distribution of \(X\) directly. You do not first have to derive the full distribution of \(g(X)\). This is often the shortest path to moments and variances.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Variance can be computed using LOTUS through \(E(X^2)\).
  • Moments are expectations of powers and therefore are direct applications of LOTUS.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Dunif}\{-1,1\}\) and \(g(x)=x^4\), then \(E(g(X))=1\).
  • If \(X\) has PMF \(p_X\), then \(E((X-E X)^2)=\sum_x (x-E X)^2p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A median of a random variable \(X\) is a number \(c\) such that

\[ P(X\le c)\ge \frac12\quad\text{and}\quad P(X\ge c)\ge\frac12. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A median is a value that splits the distribution into two sides, each with probability at least one half. It need not be unique. In contrast to the mean, the median is determined by probabilities on either side, not by the numerical size of extreme values.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Any value minimizing \(E|X-x|\) is a median, when the expectation is well-defined.
  • For a continuous strictly increasing CDF, the median is the unique solution of \(F(c)=1/2\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(1/2)\), every \(c\in[0,1]\) is a median.
  • If \(Y=e^X\) and \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(e^\mu\) is the median of \(Y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A nonnegative random variable \(X\) has the memoryless property if, for all \(s,t\ge0\) with \(P(X\ge s)>0\),

\[ P(X-s\ge t\mid X\ge s)=P(X\ge t). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Memorylessness says that knowing the event has not occurred yet does not change the distribution of the additional waiting time. In continuous time, the exponential distribution has this property; in discrete repeated-trial settings, the geometric distribution has the analogous property.

This does not mean that long waits are common. It means that after conditioning on survival up to time \(s\), the remaining waiting time restarts probabilistically.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{Expo}(\lambda)\), then \(P(X>s+t\mid X>s)=P(X>t)\).
  • In a Poisson process, memorylessness makes interarrival times independent exponential random variables.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a radioactive particle has not decayed by time \(s\), the distribution of the additional time to decay is still exponential with the same rate.
  • If an offer must exceed \(18,000\) and offers have an exponential tail, the excess above \(18,000\) behaves like a new exponential random variable.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(T_1,\ldots,T_n\) are independent and \(T_i\sim\operatorname{Expo}(\lambda_i)\), then

\[ \min_{1\le i\le n}T_i\sim\operatorname{Expo}\left(\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i\right). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Think of each \(T_i\) as a separate clock. The minimum is the first clock to ring. Since each clock has its own rate, the combined rate is the sum of all rates. More possible sources of arrivals means a shorter expected time to the first arrival.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(P(\min_i T_i>t)=\prod_i P(T_i>t)=e^{-t\sum_i\lambda_i}\).
  • The expected minimum waiting time is \(1/(\sum_i\lambda_i)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If three independent servers receive first requests with rates \(2\), \(3\), and \(5\), then the first request among all servers occurs after an \(\operatorname{Expo}(10)\) waiting time.
  • If \(n\) particles decay independently with rate \(\lambda\), the first decay time is exponential with rate \(n\lambda\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A mixture distribution chooses between component distributions using random or fixed weights. In the two-component case, if \(Y\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\) and the chosen value is \(X_1\) when \(Y=1\) and \(X_2\) when \(Y=0\), then the CDF is

\[ F(x)=pF_1(x)+(1-p)F_2(x). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A mixture is useful when the population consists of subgroups or regimes. First a component is chosen, and then a value is drawn from that component. The final distribution is not generally the same type as the components; for example, a mixture of two Poisson distributions is usually not itself Poisson.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A convex combination of CDFs, \(pF_1+(1-p)F_2\) with \(0\le p\le1\), is again a valid CDF.
  • Conditional distributions naturally produce mixtures through the law of total probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y|X=0\sim\operatorname{Pois}(1)\) and \(Y|X=1\sim\operatorname{Pois}(3)\), then the unconditional distribution of \(Y\) is a mixture of two Poisson distributions.
  • If a customer is from group 1 with probability \(p\) and group 2 otherwise, total demand can be modelled as a mixture of the two group-specific demand distributions.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A mode of a distribution is a value at which the PMF or PDF reaches its maximum value.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The mode describes the most likely point for a discrete distribution, or the peak of the density for a continuous distribution. For continuous distributions, the mode is about density height, not point probability, because individual points have probability zero.

A distribution can have no unique mode, one mode, or several modes.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A distribution with one mode is called unimodal; one with several modes is called multimodal.
  • For a monotone transformation of a discrete random variable, modes transform directly; for continuous variables, density scaling must be considered.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bern}(p)\), the mode is \(1\) if \(p>1/2\), \(0\) if \(p<1/2\), and both \(0\) and \(1\) if \(p=1/2\).
  • If \(Y=e^X\) with \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then the mode is \(e^{\mu-\sigma^2}\), not \(e^\mu\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a real-valued random variable \(X\), the \(n\)th moment is

$$ E[X^n], $$ provided the expectation exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Moments are deterministic numbers calculated from a distribution. They summarize aspects of the distribution. The first moment is the mean. Higher moments contain information about spread and shape, especially when centered or standardized.

Moments are not the same as sample moments. A moment belongs to the theoretical distribution; a sample moment is computed from observed random variables and is itself random before the data are observed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The first moment \(E[X]\) is the mean when it exists.
  • Moments can often be computed using LOTUS once the distribution of \(X\) is known.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\), the first moment is \(E[X]=\lambda\).
  • For \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), \(E[Z^2]=1\).

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
If \(X\ge Y\) with probability one and the expectations exist, then

\[ E(X)\ge E(Y). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If one random quantity is always at least as large as another, then its average cannot be smaller. The phrase “with probability one” allows exceptions only on events of probability zero.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\ge0\) with probability one, then \(E(X)\ge0\).
  • Monotonicity is the expectation step behind many probability bounds, including Chebyshev-type arguments.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Since \((X-\mu)^2\ge0\), the variance of \(X\) is nonnegative.
  • If \(0\le X\le1\), then \(X^2\le X\), hence \(E(X^2)\le E(X)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The multiplication rule says that if one task can be done in \(a\) ways and, after each of those choices, a second task can be done in \(b\) ways, then the two-step task can be done in \(ab\) ways.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Use this rule for ordered procedures: first choose something, then choose the next thing, and so on. The number of choices may change from step to step.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(r\) steps with \(n_1,n_2,\ldots,n_r\) available choices, the total number of ordered outcomes is \(n_1n_2\cdots n_r\).
  • The rule is the counting basis behind factorials and permutations.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If there are 3 choices for a first position, then 2 remaining choices for a second position, there are \(3\cdot2=6\) ordered choices.
  • Seven independent games with three possible results per game have \(3^7\) ordered result sequences.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
If all outcomes in a finite sample space \(S\) are equally likely, then the naive probability of an event \(A\subseteq S\) is

\[ P(A)=\frac{|A|}{|S|}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Naive probability is probability by counting. It is powerful when outcomes are finite and symmetric, but it is not automatically valid for every finite sample space. The main modelling step is to choose outcomes that are genuinely equally likely.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Naive probability satisfies the axioms of probability.
  • The denominator counts all equally likely outcomes; the numerator counts favourable outcomes.
  • Many counting tools, such as permutations and combinations, exist to compute these two quantities.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die, \(P(\text{even})=3/6=1/2\).
  • For a five-card poker hand, the sample space has \(\binom{52}{5}\) equally likely hands, so probabilities can be computed by counting favourable hands.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
In this course convention, a random variable \(X\) has the negative binomial distribution with parameters \(r\) and \(p\), written \(X\sim\operatorname{NBin}(r,p)\), if it counts the number of failures before the \(r\)th success:

\[ P(X=n)=\binom{n+r-1}{r-1}p^r(1-p)^n, \qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The negative binomial distribution is a waiting-time count in repeated Bernoulli trials. The value \(n\) means that before the \(r\)th success occurs, exactly \(n\) failures were observed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim\operatorname{NBin}(r,p)\), then \(E(X)=r(1-p)/p\).
  • Its variance is \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=r(1-p)/p^2\).
  • It generalizes the geometric distribution from waiting for one success to waiting for a fixed number of successes.
  • Different textbooks use different support conventions, so the parameterization should always be checked.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• With repeated independent sales attempts, the number of failures before the third sale can be modelled as negative binomial.
  • When \(r=1\), the negative binomial distribution becomes the geometric distribution under the course convention.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has a normal distribution with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2>0\) if its density is

\[ f_X(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\left(-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The normal distribution is a bell-shaped continuous distribution. Its location is controlled by \(\mu\) and its spread by \(\sigma\). It is important because standardized sums and averages often behave approximately normally.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\sigma^2\).
  • If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)\).
  • Linear transformations of normal random variables are normal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(P(|Y-\mu|<1.96\sigma)=0.95\) approximately, giving the random interval \((Y-1.96\sigma,Y+1.96\sigma)\) for \(\mu\) in the one-observation setup.
  • If \(X,Y,Z\) are independent \(N(0,1)\) variables, then \(X+2Y-2Z\sim N(0,9)\), so \(P(X+2Y<2Z+3)=\Phi(1)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
An order statistic is a random variable obtained by sorting a sample. If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are observed values, the sorted values are commonly written

\[ X_{(1)}\le X_{(2)}\le\cdots\le X_{(n)}. \]

Here \(X_{(1)}\) is the minimum and \(X_{(n)}\) is the maximum.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: For independent continuous random variables with the same distribution, ties have probability zero. Therefore all \(n!\) strict orderings are equally likely. This gives simple probabilities for relative ranks before one studies the full distribution of order statistics.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. continuous random variables, then \(P(X_1<X_2<\cdots<X_n)=1/n!\).
  • If \(U_1,\ldots,U_n\) are i.i.d. \(\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\) and \(M=\max(U_1,\ldots,U_n)\), then \(F_M(x)=x^n\) for \(0<x<1\) and \(E[M]=n/(n+1)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Among \(j\) i.i.d. continuous observations, each observation is equally likely to be the minimum, so \(P(X_j=\min_{1\le i\le j}X_i)=1/j\).
  • If \(U_1,U_2,U_3\) are independent uniform variables on \((0,1)\), then \(P(U_1<U_2<U_3)=1/6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: An outcome is a single possible result of a random experiment; outcomes are the elements of the sample space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Outcomes are the atoms of the model: after the random experiment is performed, exactly one outcome from \(S\) is treated as the realised result. What counts as one outcome depends on the level of detail in the model.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• An event occurs precisely when the realised outcome belongs to that event.
  • If \(S\) is finite and all outcomes are equally likely, each outcome has probability \(1/|S|\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In one coin toss with \(S=\{H,T\}\), the outcomes are \(H\) and \(T\).
  • In a seven-game chess model, one outcome can be \(WWDDLWL\), meaning the ordered sequence of results across all games.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A partition of a sample space \(S\) is a collection of events \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) such that the events are pairwise disjoint and their union is \(S\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A partition is a complete case split: exactly one of the cases occurs. Partitions let probability calculations be broken into smaller conditional calculations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(A_1,A_2,\ldots\) form a partition, then \(\sum_i P(A_i)=1\).
  • Partitions are the structural assumption behind the law of total probability.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(A\) and \(A^c\) form a two-part partition of \(S\).
  • In one chess game, the events win, draw, and loss form a partition of the possible results.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A permutation is an ordered arrangement or ordered selection of objects.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Use permutations when the order matters. Choosing Alice then Bob is different from choosing Bob then Alice if the positions or sequence are part of the outcome.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The number of ways to order all \(n\) distinct objects is \(n!\).
  • The number of ordered selections of \(k\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects is \(\frac{n!}{(n-k)!}\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The ordered outcome \(ABC\) is different from \(ACB\) when three apples are assigned to first, second, and third positions.
  • The number of possible ordered podiums from 8 competitors is \(8\cdot7\cdot6\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has a Poisson distribution with parameter \(\lambda>0\) if

\[ P(X=k)=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k=0,1,2,\ldots. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The Poisson distribution models counts of rare or randomly scattered events when the average count is \(\lambda\). It is central in arrival models and appears as a limit of binomial counts with many trials and small success probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(E[X]=\lambda\).
  • \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=\lambda\).
  • If \(X\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\) and \(Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\mu)\) are independent, then \(X+Y\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda+\mu)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The number of arrivals in a time interval of length \(t\) in a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\) has distribution \(\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\).
  • If calls from two independent sources have Poisson means \(2\) and \(5\), then the total number of calls has Poisson mean \(7\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A counting process \(\{N_t:t\ge0\}\) is a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda>0\) if it has independent increments and

$$ N_{t+s}-N_s\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t) $$ for all \(s,t\ge0\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A Poisson process models arrivals over time at a constant average rate. Counts over non-overlapping time intervals are independent, and the number of arrivals depends only on the length of the interval.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(N_t\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda t)\).
  • The waiting time to the first arrival is \(\operatorname{Exp}(\lambda)\).
  • The minimum of independent exponential clocks is exponential with rate equal to the sum of the rates.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If customers arrive according to a Poisson process with rate \(\lambda\), then the probability of exactly \(k\) customers in \([0,t]\) is \(e^{-\lambda t}(\lambda t)^k/k!\).
  • If many independent rare decay indicators are considered while the total expected rate is fixed, the limiting number of decays in \([0,t]\) has a Poisson distribution with mean \(\lambda t\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A probability density function of a continuous random variable \(X\) is a function \(f_X\) with \(f_X(x)\ge0\) such that

\[ F_X(x)=P(X\le x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f_X(t)\,dt. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A density is not probability at a point; it is probability per unit length. Probabilities are areas under the density curve. This is why \(f_X(x)\) can be greater than one while probabilities remain between zero and one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} f_X(x)\,dx=1\).
  • \(P(a<X\le b)=\int_a^b f_X(x)\,dx\).
  • If \(F_X\) is differentiable at \(x\), then \(f_X(x)=F_X'(x)\).
  • For continuous \(X\), \(P(X=x)=0\) for every fixed \(x\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The uniform density on \((a,b)\) is \(f(x)=1/(b-a)\) on the interval and \(0\) elsewhere.
  • The standard normal density is \(\varphi(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2}\), a bell-shaped density centered at \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A probability function is a function \(P\) that assigns a number \(P(A)\) to each event \(A\) and satisfies the axioms of probability.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A probability function is the part of the model that says how likely events are. The sample space lists what can happen; the probability function assigns consistent numerical weights to those possibilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A probability function always takes values in \([0,1]\).
  • For fixed \(B\) with \(P(B)>0\), the conditional probability \(P(\cdot\mid B)\) is again a probability function.
  • For a random variable, its distribution is the probability function induced on numerical events.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A fair die model has \(P(\{1\})=\cdots=P(\{6\})=1/6\).
  • A continuous probability model can assign probability to intervals while every single point has probability \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a discrete random variable \(X\), the probability mass function is

\[ p_X(x)=P(X=x). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A PMF puts probability directly on individual values. Values outside the support have mass zero, and all masses on the support add to one.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(p_X(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\).
  • \(\sum_x p_X(x)=1\).
  • For any set \(A\), \(P(X\in A)=\sum_{x\in A}p_X(x)\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a fair die roll, \(p_X(i)=1/6\) for \(i=1,\ldots,6\) and \(0\) otherwise.
  • For \(X\sim\operatorname{Bin}(n,p)\), the PMF is \(P(X=k)=\binom{n}{k}p^k(1-p)^{n-k}\) for \(k=0,\ldots,n\).

docs.title: Description
docs.text: The prosecutors fallacy is the error of treating a small probability of evidence under one hypothesis, such as \(P(E\mid H)\), as if it were the probability of that hypothesis given the evidence, \(P(H\mid E)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The fallacy confuses the direction of conditioning. Evidence can be rare under innocence, but the probability of innocence given the evidence also depends on the prior probability of innocence and on how likely the evidence is under alternative explanations.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(P(E\mid H)\) and \(P(H\mid E)\) are generally different.
  • Bayes rule shows that posterior probabilities require comparison between competing hypotheses.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A rare medical-test result does not automatically mean the tested condition is likely; the base rate matters.
  • If a probability model assumes two events are independent when they may share a common cause, the resulting probability can be much too small.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a CDF \(F\), a quantile function is an inverse-type function that maps probabilities \(u\in(0,1)\) to values \(x\) such that \(F(x)\) reaches probability level \(u\).

When \(F\) is continuous and strictly increasing, the quantile function is simply \(F^{-1}(u)\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Quantiles answer questions of the form: “what value cuts off a given cumulative probability?” A median is a \(0.5\)-quantile. Quartiles are \(0.25\), \(0.5\), and \(0.75\) quantiles.

The quantile function also gives a direct construction of random variables: if \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)\), then \(F^{-1}(U)\) has CDF \(F\) under the usual regularity conditions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(X\sim\operatorname{Rayleigh}(1)\) with \(F(x)=1-e^{-x^2/2}\) for \(x>0\), the quartiles are \(q_j=\sqrt{-2\log(1-j/4)}\).
  • For \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), the \(0.975\) quantile is approximately \(1.96\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The median of \(Y=e^X\) with \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) is \(e^\mu\) because \(P(Y\le e^\mu)=P(X\le\mu)=1/2\).
  • For \(U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(a,b)\), the \(p\)-quantile is \(a+p(b-a)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A random interval is an interval whose endpoints are random variables, for example \((a(Y),b(Y))\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A random interval is not a fixed set before the data are observed. Its endpoints depend on a random observation. Statements such as \(P(\mu\in(a(Y),b(Y)))=0.95\) describe the long-run probability that the random construction covers the fixed parameter \(\mu\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\) and \(\sigma\) is known, then \(P(Y-1.96\sigma<\mu<Y+1.96\sigma)\approx0.95\).
  • Rearranging inequalities can turn a probability statement about \(Y-\mu\) into a coverage statement about \(\mu\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Since \(P(|Y-\mu|<1.96\sigma)=0.95\) approximately, the interval \((Y-1.96\sigma,Y+1.96\sigma)\) covers \(\mu\) with probability about \(0.95\).
  • If \(Y=10\) and \(\sigma=2\), the realized interval is approximately \((6.08,13.92)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A random variable is a function \(X:S\to\mathbb{R}\) from the sample space to the real numbers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A random variable does not create randomness by itself. The underlying experiment produces an outcome \(s\), and the random variable converts that outcome into a number \(X(s)\). This lets us ask numerical probability questions such as \(P(X=3)\), \(P(X\le 5)\), or \(P(X\in [0,1])\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Events involving \(X\) are preimages: \(\{X\in C\}=\{s\in S:X(s)\in C\}\).
  • The distribution of \(X\) determines all probabilities of events generated by \(X\).
  • Different random variables can be defined on the same sample space to extract different information from the same experiment.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Toss ten coins and let \(X\) be the number of heads. Then \(X\) can take values \(0,1,\ldots,10\), and \(\{X=6\}\) is the event that exactly six heads occur.
  • Roll a die and let \(Y\) be \(1\) if the result is even and \(0\) otherwise. Then \(Y\) is a numerical summary of the outcome, even though the original outcome is one of six die faces.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A random variable \(X\) has the Rayleigh distribution with scale \(1\) if it has density

\[ f_X(x)=xe^{-x^2/2},\qquad x>0, \]

and \(f_X(x)=0\) otherwise.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Rayleigh distribution is a continuous distribution on positive values. It often appears as a magnitude or distance-type distribution. In this course, it is mainly useful for practicing how CDFs, quantiles, expectations, and transformations work for continuous random variables.

The CDF is especially convenient: for \(x>0\), \(F_X(x)=1-e^{-x^2/2}\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X\) has the scale-\(1\) Rayleigh distribution, then \(E[X]=\sqrt{\pi/2}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(X)=2-\pi/2\).
  • Its quartiles solve \(1-e^{-q_j^2/2}=j/4\), so \(q_j=\sqrt{-2\log(1-j/4)}\).
  • A Rayleigh random variable can arise as the length of a two-dimensional vector with independent centered normal coordinates.
  • Its CDF has the simple form \(1-e^{-x^2/(2\sigma^2)}\) for \(x\ge0\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(P(1<X<3)=F_X(3)-F_X(1)=e^{-1/2}-e^{-9/2}\).
  • If \(Y=\mu+\sigma X\) with \(\sigma>0\), then \(E[Y]=\mu+\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(Y)=\sigma^2(2-\pi/2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For observations \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with sample mean \(\bar X_n\), the \(k\)th sample central moment is

\[ \bar M_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X_n)^k. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Sample central moments measure deviations from the sample mean rather than from the theoretical mean. This makes them directly computable from data, but also means they have different algebraic properties from the corresponding theoretical central moments.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The second sample central moment with denominator \(n\) is \(\bar M_2=\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\).
  • The usual sample variance rescales \(\bar M_2\) by \(n/(n-1)\) to correct bias under i.i.d. sampling.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If all observations are equal, then every positive sample central moment is \(0\).
  • If the observations are spread far from \(\bar X_n\), then \(\bar M_2\) is large.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), the sample mean is

\[ \bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The sample mean averages observed values. Before observation, it is a random variable because it depends on the random sample. For i.i.d. observations with mean \(\mu\), the sample mean is centered at \(\mu\) and becomes less variable as \(n\) grows.

This is the mathematical version of the intuition that repeated fair coin tossing gives a sample proportion of heads closer and closer to the true success probability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. with \(E[X_i]=\mu\), then \(E[\bar X_n]=\mu\).
  • If the variables are independent with variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X_i\) is \(1\) for a head and \(0\) for a tail, then \(\bar X_n\) is the proportion of heads in \(n\) tosses.
  • If \(X_i\) are i.i.d. with mean \(0\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(E[\bar X_n]=0\) and \(\operatorname{Var}(\bar X_n)=\sigma^2/n\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For i.i.d. random variables \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), the \(k\)th sample moment is

\[ M_k=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n X_i^k. \]

The first sample moment \(M_1\) is the sample mean \(\bar X_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A sample moment is computed from a random sample. Before the sample is observed, it is a random variable. After observation, it becomes a numerical summary of the realized data.

Sample moments are empirical analogues of theoretical moments. As the sample size grows, they often become more stable and can approximate the corresponding population moments.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(M_1=\bar X_n=\frac1n\sum_i X_i\).
  • Sample moments are random variables, while theoretical moments are deterministic numbers determined by the distribution.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For Bernoulli observations, \(\bar X_n\) is the sample proportion of successes.
  • If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are observed values, \(M_2=\frac1n\sum_i X_i^2\) averages their squares.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A sample space \(S\) is the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The sample space fixes the level of detail of the model. For the same real-world situation, several sample spaces may be possible; the useful one is the one whose outcomes contain exactly the information needed for the probability questions being asked. In naive probability, it is especially important that the chosen outcomes are equally likely, otherwise counting outcomes gives misleading probabilities.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The event that something happens is the whole sample space \(S\), so \(P(S)=1\).
  • Every event is a subset of \(S\).
  • Changing the sample space can change which outcomes are equally likely, even when the real experiment is the same.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For two coin tosses, \(S=\{HH,HT,TH,TT\}\) is a detailed equally likely sample space.
  • For seven chess games with outcomes win, draw, or loss, one useful sample space is all strings of length \(7\) over \(\{W,D,L\}\).
  • For measuring a lifetime, the sample space might be \([0,\infty)\) rather than a finite set.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The sample standard deviation is the nonnegative square root of the sample variance:

\[ S_n=\sqrt{S_n^2}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The sample standard deviation measures spread in the same units as the original observations. This makes it easier to interpret than sample variance, which is measured in squared units.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• \(S_n\ge0\) always.
  • \(S_n=0\) exactly when all sample observations are equal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If all observed values are \(5\), then \(S_n=0\).
  • If the observations are measured in euros, then \(S_n\) is also measured in euros, while \(S_n^2\) is measured in squared euros.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For observations \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) with sample mean \(\bar X_n\) and sample standard deviation \(S_n\), the \(k\)th sample standardized moment is

\[ \bar M_{S,k}=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{(X_i-\bar X_n)^k}{S_n^k}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Sample standardized moments describe empirical shape after removing the sample location and scale. They are sample-based analogues of theoretical standardized moments.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For \(k=3\), the sample standardized moment is a sample analogue of skewness.
  • For \(k=4\), it is a sample analogue of kurtosis before subtracting the normal benchmark \(3\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If a sample has a long right tail, its third sample standardized moment is often positive.
  • If \(S_n=0\), standardized sample moments are not well-defined because there is no sample spread to divide by.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For observations \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\), the sample variance used in this course is

\[ S_n^2=\frac1{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (X_i-\bar X_n)^2. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The sample variance measures the spread of observations around their sample mean. The denominator is \(n-1\) rather than \(n\) because the sample mean has already been estimated from the same data. This correction makes \(S_n^2\) an unbiased estimator of the population variance under i.i.d. sampling.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(X_1,\ldots,X_n\) are i.i.d. with variance \(\sigma^2\), then \(E[S_n^2]=\sigma^2\).
  • The identity \(\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X_n-\mu)^2\) is useful for proving unbiasedness.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For a sample with no spread, \(S_n^2=0\).
  • If \(X_i\) are i.i.d. with mean \(\mu\) and variance \(\sigma^2\), the expected value of \(\frac1n\sum_i(X_i-\bar X_n)^2\) is smaller than \(\sigma^2\), which is why the \(n-1\) denominator is used for \(S_n^2\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Skewness is the third standardized moment,

\[ \operatorname{Skew}(X)=E\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^3\right], \]

and kurtosis is based on the fourth standardized moment. In this course, excess kurtosis is written as

\[ \operatorname{Kurt}(X)=E\left[\left(\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\right)^4\right]-3. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Skewness describes asymmetry. Positive skewness is associated with a longer or heavier right tail; negative skewness is associated with a longer or heavier left tail. Kurtosis describes aspects of tail weight and peak behavior relative to the normal-distribution benchmark, where subtracting \(3\) makes the normal excess kurtosis equal to \(0\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Symmetric distributions typically have skewness \(0\) when the third standardized moment exists.
  • Skewness and kurtosis are dimensionless because the deviations are standardized by \(\sigma\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• A lognormal distribution is right-skewed: its right tail pulls the mean above the median.
  • The standard normal distribution has skewness \(0\) and excess kurtosis \(0\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The standard normal distribution is the normal distribution \(N(0,1)\) with density

\[ \varphi(z)=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-z^2/2},\qquad z\in\mathbb{R}. \]

Its CDF is denoted by \(\Phi(z)=\int_{-\infty}^z\varphi(t)\,dt\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The standard normal distribution is the reference scale for all normal distributions. Standardization converts any normal random variable into this scale, so probabilities can be written using \(\Phi\).

Its density is symmetric around \(0\), so values equally far left and right of \(0\) have the same density. This gives useful identities such as \(\Phi(-z)=1-\Phi(z)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(Z\sim N(0,1)\), then \(-Z\) has the same distribution as \(Z\).
  • If \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \(P(a<X\le b)=\Phi((b-\mu)/\sigma)-\Phi((a-\mu)/\sigma)\).
  • The standard normal distribution has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\).
  • Standardization converts any non-degenerate normal random variable to a standard normal random variable.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Standardization transforms a random variable \(X\) with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma>0\) into

\[ Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Standardization measures how many standard deviations a value lies above or below the mean. It removes the original unit of measurement and places the variable on a comparable scale.

For normal variables, standardization is especially powerful: if \(X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), then \((X-\mu)/\sigma\sim N(0,1)\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(E[X]=\mu\) and \(\operatorname{SD}(X)=\sigma\), then the standardized variable has mean \(0\) and variance \(1\) when these quantities exist.
  • Normal probabilities can be converted to standard normal probabilities by subtracting \(\mu\) and dividing by \(\sigma\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• If \(X\sim N(10,4)\), then \(P(X\le 13)=\Phi((13-10)/2)=\Phi(1.5)\).
  • If a value is two standard deviations above the mean, its standardized score is \(2\).
