docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(n,\,k \in\mathbb N^+\). A function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to \mathbb{R}^k\) is termed a linear transformation/map if it is a homogeneous linear function, i.e., a function that can be represented as \(\boldsymbol f(\boldsymbol x)=\boldsymbol A \boldsymbol x,\) where \(\boldsymbol A\in\mathbb R^{k\times n}\) is a \(k\times n\) real-valued matrix. In particular, a linear transformation from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a homogeneous polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) with terms all of degree one, i.e., it has the general expression $$ f(x_1,\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)=a_1x_1+a_2x_2+\cdots+a_nx_n. $$

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A linear transformation upholds vector addition and scalar multiplication, e.g., for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \mathbb{R}^n\) and \(c \in \mathbb{R}\), it holds: $$ \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}+\boldsymbol{y}) = \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}) + \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{y}), \quad \boldsymbol{f}(c\boldsymbol{x}) = c\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}), $$

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The graph of a linear transformation from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a hyperplane of dimension \(n\) that goes through the origin.
  • Level sets of linear transformations from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}\) are a collection of parallel hyperplanes.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=x+y\) is a linear transformation.
  • \(f(x,y,z)=x-y+2z+1\) is not a linear transformation.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The maximum norm of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_\infty=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i|. \]

Correspondingly, the Chebyshev distance between \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ d_\infty(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\max_{1\leq i\leq n}|x_i-y_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The maximum norm is the limiting case of the \(p\)-norm when \(p\to+\infty\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball in the maximum norm is an axis-aligned hypercube
\[ \overline{\boldsymbol B}_{d_\infty}(\boldsymbol 0,1)=[-1,1]^n. \]

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d)\) consists of a set of points \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and a distance function (or metric) \(d\colon \boldsymbol{X} \times \boldsymbol{X} \to [0,+\infty)\) that maps pairs of points to nonnegative real values. The metric adheres to the following properties:

  1. Non-negativity: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \geq 0\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  2. Identity of indiscernibles: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{y}\text{.}\)
  3. Symmetry: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{x})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)
  4. Triangle inequality: \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{z}) \leq d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) + d(\boldsymbol{y},\boldsymbol{z})\) for any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}, \boldsymbol{z} \in \boldsymbol{X}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A metric space is just a set of points with a clear and reasonable rule for measuring the distance between any two of them.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Metrics are always nonnegative. The only point at a zero distance from a point \(\boldsymbol{x}\) is \(\boldsymbol{x}\) itself.
  • Metrics are symmetric and adhere to the triangle inequality.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance in \(\mathbb{R}^n\) is defined as \(\displaystyle d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y}) = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2\right)^{1/2}\text{.}\)
  • The complex numbers \(\mathbb{C}\) with the distance function (based on modulus) \(d(z,w) = |z-w|\) form a metric space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a function from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) is a product of real coefficients and variables raised to nonnegative integer powers, i.e., a monomial has the general expression

\[ f(x_1,x_2,\dots,x_n) = a x_1^{k_1} x_2^{k_2} \cdots x_n^{k_n}, \]

with constant \(a \in \mathbb{R}\) and exponents \(k_1,\, \dots,\, k_n \in \mathbb{N}\). The total degree of a monomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is the sum of the exponents of all variables appearing in that monomial, i.e., \(k_1+\cdots+k_n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A monomial is a simple expression made by multiplying a constant with each variable raised to a whole number power.

Its total degree is the sum of those powers, telling you how many factors of variables appear in total.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The product of two monomials is again a monomial. The exponents add componentwise, and the constant multiplies.
  • Every monomial is a homogeneous function whose degree equals its total degree.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y)=-2x^2y\)  is a monomial with exponents \(k_1=2\), \(k_2=1\), total degree \(3\).
  • The monomial \(f(x,y)=x^4\) has \(k_1=4\), \(k_2=0\), total degree \(4\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A norm on a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}\) (commonly \(\mathbb{R}\)) is a function \(\|\cdot\|\colon \boldsymbol{V}\to[0,+\infty)\) that adheres to the following criteria:

  1. Non-negativity and definiteness: For any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| \geq 0\), and \(\|\boldsymbol{x}\| = 0\) if and only if \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{0}\).
  2. Positive homogeneity: For any scalar \(c \in \mathbb{F}\) and any \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{V}\), \(\|c\boldsymbol{x}\| = |c|\cdot\|\boldsymbol{x}\|\).
  3. Triangle inequality: For any \(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{V}\): \(\|\boldsymbol{x} + \boldsymbol{y}\| \leq \|\boldsymbol{x}\| + \|\boldsymbol{y}\|\).

A normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\) is a vector space \(\boldsymbol{V}\) over the scalar field \(\mathbb{F}\) (commonly \(\mathbb{R}\)), equipped with a norm \(\|\cdot\|\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A norm is a rule that assigns a length to every vector in a consistent way.

A normed vector space is just a vector space where every vector has such a length, and scaling or adding vectors behaves as you would expect.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Given a normed vector space \((\boldsymbol{V}, \|\cdot\|)\), one can define the metric as \(d(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) = \|\boldsymbol{x} - \boldsymbol{y}\|,\) making \((\boldsymbol{V}, d)\) inherently a metric space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The real line \(\mathbb{R}\) with the absolute-value norm forms a normed vector space over \(\mathbb{R}\).
  • The plane \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the Euclidean norm is similarly a normed vector space. Using the taxicab norm, \(\mathbb{R}^2\) remains a normed vector space.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\). We say the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\) is normally convergent if the series of uniform norms of the terms of the series converges, i.e., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Normal convergence means the functions are so well controlled that their worst-case contributions are summable.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Normal convergence implies uniform absolute convergence, which in turn implies uniform convergence, which in turn implies pointwise convergence, i.e.,
\[ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty<+\infty\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\rightrightarrows f\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\;\implies\; \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\to f. \]

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Uniform absolute convergence does not imply normal convergence. Consider $\(f(x)=\begin{cases} \displaystyle \, 1/n, &x=n,\\[2pt] \displaystyle \, 0, &x\neq n.\end{cases}\)$Then the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |f_n(x)|\) is uniformly convergent, however the series of uniform norms is the harmonic series and thus diverges.

docs.title: Open and Closed Sets in a Metric Space
Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and its subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\):

  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is closed if it includes all of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{E}\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if it doesn't include any of its boundary points, i.e., \(\partial \boldsymbol{E} \cap \boldsymbol{E} = \varnothing\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is neither open nor closed if it includes some but not all of its boundary points.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Open sets keep their boundaries out. Closed sets keep their boundaries in. Sets that include some boundary points but not others are neither open nor closed.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if \(\boldsymbol{E} = \mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol F\) is closed if and only if every convergent sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^{\infty}\) within \(\boldsymbol{F}\) converges to a limiting point lying in \(\boldsymbol{F}\).
  • A set \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is open if and only if its complement \(\boldsymbol{E}^\complement=\boldsymbol{X}\setminus \boldsymbol{E}\) is closed.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0, \varepsilon)\) is open.
  • \(\varnothing\) is both open and closed. It has no boundary points to include or exclude.
  • Under the discrete metric, every set is both open and closed. Each singleton set has a ball containing only itself.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\), a point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), and \(r > 0\), the open metric ball \(\boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) in \(\boldsymbol{X}\), centered at \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) with radius \(r\) in metric \(d\), is defined as the following set:

\[ \boldsymbol{B}_{(\boldsymbol{X},d)}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r) = \{\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{X} \colon d(\boldsymbol{x}, \boldsymbol{x}_0) < r\}. \]

If the context is clear, we'll abbreviate this as \(\boldsymbol{B}_d(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r)\) or simply \(\boldsymbol{B}(\boldsymbol{x}_0,r).\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
An open metric ball is the set of all points whose distance from the center is strictly less than the radius.

It is the basic building block for defining open sets and continuity in metric spaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Open balls are open sets.
  • A subset of a metric space is open if and only if it can be written as a union of open balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with the usual distance, \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is the open disc of radius \(1\) centered at the origin. Points with \(x^2 + y^2 < 1\) are elements of this ball.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}^2\) with \(d_1\), \(\boldsymbol B((0,0),1)\) is a diamond shape with vertices at \((\pm1,0)\) and \((0,\pm1)\).
  • In any set with the discrete metric, \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,1) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\) and \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,0.5) = \{\boldsymbol x\}\), but \(\boldsymbol B(\boldsymbol x,2)\) is the whole space.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1,x_2, \ldots,x_n)\in\mathbb{R}^n\). For \(p\in[1,+\infty]\), the \(\boldsymbol{p}\)-norm, denoted \(\|\cdot\|_p\), is defined on \(\mathbb{R}^n\) by:

\[ \|\boldsymbol{x}\|_p = \left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

Correspondingly, the \(p\)-metric \(d_p\) is defined as

\[ d_p(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\left(\sum_{i=1}^n |x_i-y_i|^p\right)^{\frac{1}{p}}. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The \(p\)-norm is a way of measuring the size of a vector by raising each coordinate's absolute value to the \(p\)-th power, summing them, and taking the \(p\)-th root.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The smallest permissible value for \(p\) in the \(p\)-norm is \(1\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Euclidean distance \(d_2\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=2\).
  • The taxicab distance \(d_1\) is a particular \(p\)-metric when \(p=1\).
  • The maximum norm \(\|\cdot\|_\infty\) is a particular \(p\)-norm when \(p=+\infty\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) and consider a function \(\boldsymbol{f} \colon \boldsymbol{E} \to \mathbb{R}^k\). For an interior point \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\) of \(\boldsymbol{E}\) and an integer \(1 \leq j \leq n\), the partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\) with respect to the \(x_j\)-variable at \(\boldsymbol{x} = \boldsymbol{x}_0\), denoted by \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\), is given by

\[ \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \lim_{{t\to0}} \frac{\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j) - \boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)}{t} = \left.\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0 + t\boldsymbol{e}_j)\,\right|_{t=0}, \]

where \(\boldsymbol{e}_j\) represents the unit vector in the positive direction of the \(j\)-th coordinate, provided the limit exists.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The partial derivative measures how the function changes when you nudge only one coordinate while keeping all others fixed.

It is like taking an ordinary derivative in the direction of that coordinate axis.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exists if and only if both \(\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) and \(\mathrm{D}_{-\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)\) exist and are negatives of each other. In such a scenario, we have \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)=\mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{e}_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • For vector \(\displaystyle \boldsymbol{v} = (v_1,\,\ldots,\,v_n)= \sum_{j=1}^n v_j\boldsymbol{e}_j\), we have \(\displaystyle \mathrm{D}_{\boldsymbol{v}}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \sum_{j=1}^n v_j \frac{\partial }{\partial x_j}\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0).\)
  • If all the partial derivatives are both existent within a neighborhood and continuous at the center, then \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is totally differentiable at this point.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The partial derivative of \(f(x,y) = 3x^2y^2 + 4xy^3 + 7y\) with respect to the first variable is \(\dfrac{\partial }{\partial x}f(x,y) = 6xy^2 + 4y^3.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) a subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) is termed path-connected if, for any two distinct points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) a path \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{E}\) exists such that \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: You can walk from any point to any other point in a path-connected set without ever leaving the set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In the metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\text{,}\) any path-connected subset of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is connected.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The topologist's sine curve is connected but not path-connected: $$ {(0,0)}\cup {(x,\sin (1/x)) \colon x\in (0,+\infty)}. $$
  • The collection of line segments joining the origin to points \((1, 1/n)\) for all positive integers \(n\), together with the point \((1,0)\) is also connected but not path-connected.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: In a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X}, d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\), a path is a continuous function \(\boldsymbol{p}\colon [0,1] \to \boldsymbol{X}\). If for two points \(\boldsymbol{a}, \boldsymbol{b} \in \boldsymbol{X}\), the path \(\boldsymbol{p}\) satisfies \(\boldsymbol{p}(0) = \boldsymbol{a}\) and \(\boldsymbol{p}(1) = \boldsymbol{b}\), it is termed as a path from \(\boldsymbol{a}\) to \(\boldsymbol{b}\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A path is a continuous journey from one point to another within the space.

It is like drawing a curve without lifting your pencil, with the curve entirely contained in the space.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• If \(\boldsymbol p\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\) and \(\boldsymbol q\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol c\), then it is possible to construct a path from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol c\) using \(\boldsymbol p\) and \(\boldsymbol q\). This is called the concatenation.
  • For any path \(\boldsymbol p\) from \(\boldsymbol a\) to \(\boldsymbol b\), the reverse path \(\boldsymbol p(1−t)\) is a path from \(\boldsymbol b\) to \(\boldsymbol a\).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In Euclidean space, the function \(p(t)=(1−t)a+tb\) is a path from \(a\) to \(b\).
  • The function \(p(t)=(\cos⁡(2\pi t),\sin(⁡2\pi t))\) is a path from \((1,0)\) back to itself (a loop).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) be a sequence of functions \(f_n\colon X_n\to \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^{\infty}\) converges pointwise to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\to f\text{,}\) if for every \(x \in X\text{,}\) \(\displaystyle \lim _{n \rightarrow \infty} f_n(x) = f(x)\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Pointwise convergence means that for each fixed point, the function values get closer to a limit as the index goes to infinity.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Pointwise convergence guarantees that the limit exists at each individual point.
  • Pointwise convergence does not preserve boundedness, limits/continuity, differentiability, or integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=1/x\text{.}\)
  • \(f_n(x)=\dfrac{x^2}{\sqrt{x^2+1 / n}}\) converges pointwise to \(f(x)=|x|.\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The polar coordinate system specifies a given point in a plane by using two coordinates:

  • the point's distance from a reference point called the pole,
  • the point's direction from the pole relative to the direction of the polar axis, a ray drawn from the pole.

The distance from the pole is called the radius, and the angle is called the polar angle.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The polar coordinate system locates a point on a plane by saying how far away it is from a center point and what angle it makes from a fixed direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Conversion to Cartesian coordinates: \(x = r \cos \theta\), \(y = r \sin \theta.\)
  • Conversion from Cartesian coordinates: \(r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}\), \(\theta = \text{atan2}(y, x).\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\theta = \pi/4\) is a line through the pole making angle \(\pi/4\) with the polar axis.
  • \(r = 1\) is a unit circle centered at the pole.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is a real-valued function that is a finite sum of monomials on \(\mathbb R^n\). The degree of a polynomial on \(\mathbb R^n\) is is defined as the maximum, over all its monomials, of the  total degree of each monomial.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A polynomial in several variables is a finite combination of monomials added together.

Its degree is the highest total degree among all the monomials that appear with nonzero coefficient.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The degree of the sum of two polynomials is at most the maximum of their degrees. The degree of the product of two polynomials is the sum of their degrees.
  • Polynomials are infinitely differentiable. All partial derivatives of all orders exist and are themselves polynomials (or zero).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + 2xy + y^2 + x + 1\) is a polynomial of degree 2. Its highest total degree comes from \(x^2\), \(xy\), and \(y^2\), all degree 2.
  • \(f(x,y) = x^3 + xy + y^2\) has degree 3 from the \(x^3\) term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(a \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) A power series centered at \(\boldsymbol{a}\) is expressed as \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) where \((c_n)_{n=0}^\infty\) is a sequence of real numbers, independent of \(x\text{.}\) We refer to \(c_n\) as the \(\boldsymbol{n}\)-th coefficient of the power series.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A power series is an infinite sum of power functions.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • This is the formal definition of power series since it is not discussed whether such a series is convergent or divergent for different \(x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial is a special case of a power series, since the coefficients \(c_n\) are allowed to be zero.
  • \(1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+\dfrac{x^3}{6}+\cdots\) is a power series.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A quadratic form is a polynomial from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R\) with terms all of degree two, i.e., a quadratic on \(\mathbb R^n\) has the general expression:

$$ f(\boldsymbol x) = \boldsymbol{x}^\intercal \boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}= \sum_{i,j=1,\,i\leq j}^{n} a_{ij} x_i x_j. $$ where \(\boldsymbol{x}=(x_1\,x_2,\,\dots,\,x_n)^\intercal\) and \(\boldsymbol A=(a_{ij})_{1\leq i,j\leq n}\) is any nonzero \(n\times n\) matrix.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A quadratic form is a polynomial where every term has exactly two variables multiplied together, possibly the same variable squared.

It can always be written using a symmetric matrix that encodes all the coefficients.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For any quadratic form, the associated matrix is not unique. However, there always exists a unique symmetric matrix \(\overline {\boldsymbol A}=(\boldsymbol A+\boldsymbol A^\intercal)/2\) where \(\boldsymbol A\) is any associated matrix of the quadratic form.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(f(x,y) = x^2 + y^2\) is a quadratic form. Both terms are squares, degree two.
  • \(f(x,y) = 3x^2 + 4xy + 5y^2\) is a quadratic form. It includes a square term, a cross term, and another square term.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: For a given power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\text{,}\) its radius of convergence \(R\) is a nonnegative real number or \(+\infty\) such that the series converges if \(|x-a|<R\) and diverges if \(|x-a|>R\text{.}\) The interval of convergence is the set of all values of \(x\) for which the series converges.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The radius of convergence tells you how far from the center point a power series will reliably converge.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The convergence of \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) at \(x=a-R\) and \(x=a+R\) is to be determined case-by-case.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) with \(R = 1/2\) centered at \(a = 3\), converges pointwise on \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) and uniformly on any closed interval within it. Its convergence interval is \(\left(5/2, 7/2\right)\) since the series diverges at both endpoints.
  • The series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) with \(R = 0\) centered at \(a = -2\), converges solely at its center \(x = -2.\)

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n\in\mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{a_{n+1}}{a_n} \right|\text{,}\) then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\) or the limit does not exist, the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The ratio test states that a series converges if the limit of the ratio of consecutive terms is less than 1, and diverges if it is greater than 1.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • For the power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x - a)^n\text{,}\) the radius of convergence \(R\) can be found using \(\displaystyle R = \lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{c_{n}}{c_{n+1}} \right|\) if the limit exists or tends to infinity.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)/\mathrm{e}^{n+1}}{n/\mathrm{e}^n} \right| =\dfrac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n+1}/(n+1)}{2^n/n} \right| =2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!}\) converges for all \(x\in\mathbb{R}\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{(n+1)!}{n!} \right|=+\infty\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^n(x-3)^n\) converges for \(|x-3|<1/2\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{2^{n}}{2^{n+1}} \right|=\dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n!(x+1)^n\) diverges for all \(x\) except \(x=-1\) since \(\displaystyle R=\lim_{n \to \infty} \left| \dfrac{n!} {(n+1)!}\right|=0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(f\colon E \to \mathbb{R}\) be a function where \(E \subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) We say:

  • \(f\) is real analytic at \(\boldsymbol{x=a}\) if \(a\) is an interior point of \(E\) and there exists a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) centered at \(a\) and an open interval \((a-r, a+r) \subseteq E\) (for some \(r > 0\)) where this series converges to \(f\text{.}\)
  • \(f\) is real analytic on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) if \(E\) is an open set and \(f\) is real analytic at every point \(a \in E\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A function is real analytic at a point if it can be represented by a power series that matches the function exactly in a small interval around that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The convergence type here is not limited, but if we consider a closed subinterval of \((a-r,a+r)\text{,}\) then it is the uniform convergence.
  • Sums, products, and compositions of real analytic functions are also real analytic.
  • A real analytic function is always infinitely differentiable, and all of its higher-order derivatives are real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Almost all common functions are real analytic.
  • Most piecewise functions are not real analytic, though they can be even infinitely differentiable. For instance, the following function is a particular non-analytic but infinitely differentiable function.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The real coordinate space of dimension \(n\), denoted \(\mathbb {R} ^{n}\), is the set of all ordered \(n\)-tuples of real numbers.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Real coordinate space is just the collection of all points with \(n\) real coordinates.

It is the standard space used for doing multivariable calculus and linear algebra.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • With component-wise addition and scalar multiplication, the real coordinate space is a real vector space.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Special cases are called the real line \(\mathbb R^1\), the real coordinate plane \(\mathbb R^2\), and the real coordinate three-dimensional space \(\mathbb R^3\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Consider the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a_n\) where \(a_n \in \mathbb{R}\text{.}\) Let \(\displaystyle L = \limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{|a_n|}\), then:

  • If \(L < 1\text{,}\) the series converges. Moreover, \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty |a_n|\) also converges.
  • If \(L > 1\text{,}\) the series diverges.
  • If \(L = 1\text{,}\) the test is inconclusive.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The root test determines convergence by comparing the limit of the \(n\)-th root of the terms' absolute values to 1.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• One of the differences between the ratio test and the root test is that the limit in the ratio test may not exist, while the limit in the root test always exists.
  • The radius of convergence of a power series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty c_n (x-a)^n\) is given by $$ R=\frac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n\to\infty} |c_n|^{1/n}}. $$

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n}\) is convergent since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left| \frac{n}{\mathrm{e}^n} \right|} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{e}}<1\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{2^n}{n}\) diverges since \(\displaystyle L=\limsup_{n \to \infty} \sqrt[n]{\left|\frac{2^n}{n} \right|} = 2>1\text{.}\)
  • When \(L=1\text{,}\) both convergent and divergent series exist, e.g., \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n}\) diverges while \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{n^2}\) converges.
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty n(-2)^n (x-3)^n\) is convergent for \(|x-3|<\dfrac{1}{2}\) since \(R = \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \to\infty}|n\left(-2\right)^{n}|^{1/n}} = \dfrac{1}{2}\text{.}\)
  • \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{n^2} (x+2)^n\) is divergent except at \(x=-2\) since \(R= \dfrac{1}{\limsup\limits_{n \rightarrow \infty}|2^{n^{2}}|^{1/n}}= 0\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{f}\) be a twice continuously differentiable function. The second-order partial derivatives, defined as \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}\left(\frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i}\right)\), is called the \(\boldsymbol{x_ix_j}\)-second partial derivative of \(\boldsymbol{f}\). Commonly, the notation is simplified by denoting \(\partial\partial\) as \(\partial^2\), i.e., \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j \partial x_i}\), for \(i\neq j\), and \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i^2}\) for \(i=j.\) When \(i\neq j\), this second partial derivative is also referred to as the cross partial derivative or mixed partial derivative.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: A second-order partial derivative measures how the rate of change in one direction changes as you move in another direction.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If a function is twice continuously differentiable on an open set, then the mixed partials are equal.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y)=(x^2+xy,y^2)\), we have \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x^2}(x,y) = (2,0)\), \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial y\partial x}(x,y) = (1,0)\), \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x\partial y}(x,y) = (1,0)\), \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial y^2}(x,y) = (0,2)\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) be a metric space. A subset \(\boldsymbol{E}\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) is termed sequentially compact if for every sequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) with each \(\boldsymbol{x}_i \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{,}\) there exists a convergent subsequence \((\boldsymbol{x}_{i_j})_{j=1}^\infty\) that converges to a point \(\boldsymbol{x} \in \boldsymbol{E}\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A set is sequentially compact if every infinite sequence drawn from it has a subsequence that converges to a point still inside the set.

It captures the idea that the set is "closed under taking limits of subsequences."

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • In any metric space, a set is compact if and only if it is sequentially compact. This gives two equivalent ways to think about compactness: open covers or convergent subsequences.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The closed unit ball \(\{x\in \mathbb R^n\colon \|x\|\leq 1\}\) is sequentially compact. This fails in infinite dimensions.
  • Any finite set in any metric space is compact.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \(\boldsymbol{X}\) be a metric space. The metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed strongly equivalent, denoted \(d_p\approx d_q\), if positive constants \(a\) and \(b\) exist such that for any \(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y} \in \boldsymbol{X}\), $$ a \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq d_q(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}) \leq b \cdot d_p(\boldsymbol{x},\boldsymbol{y}). $$

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Equivalent metrics measure distances in different scales but agree on which points are close or far apart.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The strong equivalence relation possesses symmetry (\(d_p\approx d_q\) if and only if \(d_q\approx d_p\)), reflexivity (\(d_p\approx d_p\)) and transitivity (if \(d_p\approx d_q\) and \(d_q\approx d_r\), then \(d_p\approx d_r\)).
  • Strongly equivalent metrics induce the same notion of convergence.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any two \(p\)-metrics on \(\mathbb R^n\) are strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric, \(d_{\text{disc}}\), is not strongly equivalent to any of the \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\boldsymbol{E}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a twice-differentiable function. Then for all \(1\leq i,j\leq n\), if \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j\partial x_i}\) and \(\dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}\) are continuous at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_j\partial x_i} (\boldsymbol{x}_0) = \dfrac{\partial^2 \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i\partial x_j} (\boldsymbol{x}_0). \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If the mixed partial derivatives are continuous at a point, you can differentiate in either order and get the same result. The order of differentiation does not matter under this smoothness condition.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Clairaut's theorem guarantees that the Hessian matrix is symmetric for twice continuously differentiable functions.
  • For functions with continuous partial derivatives of order \(k\), the order of differentiation for any mixed partial of order up to \(k\) can be rearranged freely.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • Second derivatives of all smooth functions are symmetric.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The taxicab distance between points \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) and \(\boldsymbol y=(y_1,y_2,\ldots,y_n)\) in an \(n\)-dimensional real coordinate space \(\mathbb R^n\) with fixed Cartesian coordinate system is:

\[ d_1(\boldsymbol x,\boldsymbol y)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|y_i-x_i|. \]

The taxicab norm, or known as \(\ell^1\) norm, of \(\boldsymbol x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)\) is calculated as:

\[ \|\boldsymbol x\|_1=\sum_{i=1}^{n}|x_i|. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The taxicab distance represents the distance a taxi would travel between two points when restricted to cardinal directions (north, south, east, west) without moving diagonally or in any other curved path.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • The closed unit ball in the taxicab norm is an \(n\)-dimensional cross-polytope, e.g., a diamond in \(\mathbb R^2\) and a regular octahedron in \(\mathbb R^3\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The polynomial that emerges from Taylor's theorem is termed the \(\boldsymbol{k}\)-th order Taylor polynomial for the function \(f\) at \(x=a\): $$ P_{k}(x) = f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k}. $$

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial of \(f\) captures the initial \(k+1\) terms of its Taylor series (given existence) centered at the same point.
  • This polynomial stands out as the unique asymptotic best fit for the function \(f\text{.}\)

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The \(k\)-th order Taylor polynomial and the function \(f\) share the same derivatives up to the \(k\)-th order.
  • One can write a Taylor polynomial for a function just from its first few derivatives, but the full Taylor series exists if the function is smooth, and the full series converges to the function only if it's real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The 3rd order Taylor polynomial of \(\sin x\) around \(x=0\) is \(P_3(x) = x - \dfrac{x^3}{3!}\).
  • The 1st order Taylor polynomial of \(1/x\) around \(x = 1\) is \(P_1(x)=2-x\).

docs.title: Proposition
docs.text:
Let \(a\) be an interior point of \(E\subseteq \mathbb{R}\text{,}\) and let \(f\colon E\to\mathbb{R}\) be real analytic at \(x=a\text{.}\) Then \(f\) has the power series expansion around \(x=a\):

\[ f(x) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!} (x-a)^n \quad \text{for all } x \in (a-r,a+r), \]

known as the Taylor series of \(f\) around \(x=a\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: If a function is so smooth that it behaves exactly like an infinite polynomial near a point, then that polynomial is built entirely from its derivatives at that point.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Taylor series centered at the origin is called the Maclaurin series.
  • For any smooth function you can write down its Taylor series, but that series is guaranteed to converge to the function only if the function is real analytic.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The Taylor series of the natural exponential function at the origin: $$ \displaystyle \mathrm{e}^x = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} = 1 + x + \dfrac{x^2}{2!} + \dfrac{x^3}{3!} + \cdots. $$
  • The generalized binomial expansion at the origin: $$ \displaystyle (x+1)^r = \sum_{i=0}^\infty \binom{r}{i} x^i = 1 + rx + \frac{r(r-1)}{2}x^2 + \frac{r(r-1)(r-2)}{6}x^3 + \cdots. $$

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text:
Let \(k \geq 1\) be an integer and assume that the function \(f\colon \mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}\) is \(k\)-times differentiable (not necessarily real analytic) at \(x=a\text{.}\) There exists a function \(\displaystyle h_k \colon \mathbb{R} \to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\displaystyle \lim_{x\to a} h_k(x) = 0\) and

\[ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^k + R_k(x) \]

where \(R_k(x)= h_k(x)(x-a)^k\) is called the Peano form of the remainder.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: One can approximate a smooth function near a point using a polynomial, and the error term behaves like \((x−a)^k\) multiplied by something that tends to \(0\) as \(x\) approaches \(a\).

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Using the little-\(o\) notation, the statement in Taylor's theorem reads as \(R_k(x)=o((x-a)^k)\text{,}\) as \(x\to a\text{.}\) In this case, we have the \(k\)-th order Taylor expansion: $$ f(x) = f(a) + f'(a)(x-a) + \cdots + \frac{f^{(k)}(a)}{k !}(x-a)^{k} + o((x-a)^{k}). $$

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• \(\mathrm e^x=1+x+\dfrac{x^2}{2}+h_2(x)x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty \dfrac{x^{n-2}}{n!}\).
  • \(\dfrac{1}{1-x}=1+x+x^2+h_2(x) x^2\), where \(\displaystyle h_2(x)=\sum_{n=3}^\infty x^{n-2}\), for \(|x|<1\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Two metrics \(d_p\) and \(d_q\) on a space \(\boldsymbol{X}\) are termed (topologically) equivalent if they produce identical topology (the set of open subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\)) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\), i.e., a subset \(\boldsymbol{E} \subseteq \boldsymbol{X}\) is open with respect to \(d_p\) if and only if it's open under \(d_q\). This relationship is expressed as \(d_p \sim d_q.\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Two metrics are topologically equivalent if they determine the same collection of open sets.

They may measure distances differently, but they agree on which points are close enough to be in the same open set.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If two metrics are strongly equivalent, then they are topologically equivalent.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The metric \(d_{\tan}(x,y)=|\tan x-\tan y|\) is topologically equivalent to the absolute value metric on \(\mathbb R\), but they are not strongly equivalent.
  • The discrete metric is not topologically equivalent to any \(p\)-metrics.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
A topology on a set \(\boldsymbol{X}\), often denoted by \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\), is a collection of subsets of \(\boldsymbol{X}\) that satisfies the following properties:

  1. Both the empty set and the entire set \(\boldsymbol{X}\) belong to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  2. Any union of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) also belongs to \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).
  3. The intersection of any finite number of elements in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\) remains in \(\boldsymbol{\tau}\).

The pair \((\boldsymbol{X},\boldsymbol \tau)\) is called a topological space.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A topology is a collection of open sets that tells you which points are close to which without using a distance.

It is the most general setting for studying continuity and convergence.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Metric spaces are topological spaces. Every metric space induces a topology where open sets are unions of open metric balls.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The trivial topology is the topology with the least possible number of open sets, namely the empty set and the entire space, i.e., \(\boldsymbol{\tau}=\{\varnothing, \boldsymbol X\}\).

docs.title: Total Derivative as a Linear Transformation
Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\), let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function, let \(\boldsymbol{x}_0\in\mathrm{int}\boldsymbol{E}\), and let \(\boldsymbol{L}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a linear transformation. We say that \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is (totally) differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_{\boldsymbol{0}}\) with (total) derivative} \(\boldsymbol{L}\) if:

\[ \lim_{\substack{\boldsymbol{x}\to\boldsymbol{x}_0}}\frac{\|\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x})-(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_0)+\boldsymbol{L}(\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0))\|}{\|\boldsymbol{x}-\boldsymbol{x}_0\|}=0. \]

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Total differentiability means the function can be approximated near the point by a linear transformation, with the error shrinking to zero faster than the distance to the point.

It is the multidimensional version of the Newton's approximation, which is an equivalent formulation of differentiability.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• For the function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \mathbb{R}^n\to\mathbb{R}^k\) at \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\), its derivative, \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}\), is a \(k\times n\) matrix or an equivalent linear transformation from \(\mathbb{R}^n\) to \(\mathbb{R}^k\).
  • \(\mathrm{D} \boldsymbol{f}_{\boldsymbol{x}_0}(\boldsymbol{h})\), where \(\boldsymbol{h}\) is an infinitesimal vector, provides an approximation of the shift in \(\boldsymbol{f}\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^k\)) arising from the change \(\boldsymbol{h}\) in \(\boldsymbol{x}\) around \(\boldsymbol{x}=\boldsymbol{x}_0\) (a vector in \(\mathbb{R}^n\)).

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(\boldsymbol{f}(x,y) = (x^2,y^2)\) is differentiable at \(\boldsymbol{x}=(1,2)\) with the derivative \(\boldsymbol{L}(x,y) = (2x,4y)\).
  • The function \(f(x,y) = \sin(x^2+y)\) is differentiable at \((x,y)=(0,0)\) and the derivative is \(L(x,y)=y\).

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
Let \(\boldsymbol{E}\subseteq \mathbb{R}^n\) be an open set and let \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{E}\to\mathbb{R}^k\) be a function.

  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is continuously differentiable if its partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i}\) exists and remains continuous on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) for all \(1 \leq i \leq n\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is twice continuously differentiable if it's continuously differentiable and its partial derivative \(\displaystyle \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{f}}{\partial x_i}\) is also continuously differentiable on \(\boldsymbol{E}\) for all \(1\leq i\leq n\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
A continuously differentiable function has all its partial derivatives existing and varying continuously across the domain.

Twice continuously differentiable means those partial derivatives themselves have continuous partial derivatives.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • If a function is continuously differentiable on an open set, then it is totally differentiable at every point. The converse is not always true.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • All polynomials are continuously differentiable and twice continuously differentiable everywhere.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Consider metric spaces \((\boldsymbol{X},d_{\boldsymbol{X}})\) and \((\boldsymbol{Y},d_{\boldsymbol{Y}})\), and a function \(\boldsymbol{f}\colon \boldsymbol{X}\to\boldsymbol{Y}\). We say \(\boldsymbol{f}\) is uniformly continuous on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) if, for any \(\varepsilon > 0\), there exists a \(\delta > 0\) such that for all \(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2\in\boldsymbol{X}\) with \(d_{\boldsymbol{X}}(\boldsymbol{x}_1,\boldsymbol{x}_2)<\delta\), it holds that \(d_{\boldsymbol{Y}}(\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_1),\boldsymbol{f}(\boldsymbol{x}_2))<\varepsilon\).

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: This is the general definition of uniform continuity where the metric functions are allowed to be potentially different metrics on possibly different spaces.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Any continuous function defined on a compact set is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Every constant function is uniformly continuous regardless of the metrics.
  • Every function from a discrete space is uniformly continuous.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: A function \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is said to be uniformly continuous if, for every \(\varepsilon >0\text{,}\) there exists a \(\delta >0\) such that for all pairs of points \(x_1, x_2\in X\) with \(|x_1-x_2|<\delta\text{,}\) it holds that \(|f(x_1)-f(x_2)|<\varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Uniform continuity means one fixed rule for “how small is small” works everywhere, while ordinary continuity may need different rules at different points.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Every uniformly continuous function is continuous, the converse doesn't necessarily hold.
  • \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \(X\) if and only if given two equivalent sequences \((x_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((y_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) in \(X\text{,}\) sequences \((f(x_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) and \((f(y_n))_{n=1}^\infty\) are also equivalent.
  • A continuous function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a, b)\) if and only if the right limit \(\displaystyle f(a^+)\) and the left limit \(\displaystyle f(b^-)\) both exist and are finite. In other words, continuous functions can fail to be uniformly continuous if they are unbounded on a bounded domain.
  • A differentiable function \(f\) is uniformly continuous on \((a,b)\) if \(f'\) is bounded. In other words, continuous functions can fail to be uniformly continuous if their slopes become unbounded on an infinite domain.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f(x)=1/x\) is uniformly continuous on \((1,2)\), but not uniformly continuous on \((0,1)\).
  • The function \(g(x)=\sin x\) is uniformly continuous on any interval in this domain.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: Let \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) be a sequence of functions defined on \(X \subseteq \mathbb{R}\) and \(f\colon X \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be another function. We say that \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to \(\boldsymbol{f}\) on \(\boldsymbol{X}\) and write \(f_n\rightrightarrows f\text{,}\) if for every \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a positive integer \(N\) such that for all \(n > N\text{,}\) the inequality \(|f_n(x) - f(x) | < \varepsilon\) holds for all \(x \in X\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Uniform convergence means that the function values get close to the limit at the same speed for all points, not one point at a time.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Uniform convergence implies pointwise convergence.
  • Uniform convergence preserves boundedness, limits/continuity (uniform limit theorem), differentiability, and integrals.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• The function \(f_n(x) = x/n\) converges uniformly on \(\mathbb R\) to \(f(x)=0\text{.}\)
  • The function \(f_n(x) = \dfrac{n}{nx + 1}\) on \([0,1]\) converges pointwise, but not uniformly, to \(f(x)=1/x\text{.}\)

docs.title: Definition
docs.text: The uniform norm \(\|f\|_\infty\) of a bounded functions \(f\colon X \to \mathbb{R}\) is defined as: $$ |f|\infty = \sup |f(x)|. $$

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: The uniform norm is the supremum of the absolute value of the function over its entire domain.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • A sequence of functions \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) converges uniformly to a function \(f\) on \(X\) if and only if: $$ \lim_{n \to \infty} |f_n - f|_\infty = 0. $$

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• For the function \(f\colon (0,+\infty) \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(f(x) = \mathrm{e}^{-x}\), we have \(\|f\|_\infty = 1.\)
  • For the function \(g\colon \mathbb R \to \mathbb{R}\) defined by \(g(x) = \sin x\), we have \(\|g\|_\infty = 1.\)

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Closed Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of closed subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable intersection \(\displaystyle\bigcap_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite union \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also closed.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Closed sets are preserved under finite unions and arbitrary intersections.

Infinite unions can break closedness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always closed (and also open).
  • In fact any intersection of closed sets, not just countably many, is closed. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty [-1/n, 1/n] = {0}\) is closed. Shrinking closed intervals collapse to a single closed point.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty [0, 1-1/n] = [0,1)\) is not closed. It is missing the endpoint \(1\).

docs.title: Union and Intersection of Open Sets
Proposition
docs.text: For a metric space \((\boldsymbol{X},d)\) and a collection of open subsets \((\boldsymbol{E}_i)_{i=1}^\infty\) of \(\boldsymbol{X}\), the countable union \(\displaystyle\bigcup_{i=1}^\infty \boldsymbol{E}_i\) and the finite intersection \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{i=1}^k \boldsymbol{E}_i\) are also open.

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
Open sets are preserved under finite intersections and arbitrary unions.

Infinite intersections can break openness.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• Both \(X\) and \(\varnothing\) are always open (and also closed).
  • In fact any union of open sets, not just countably many, is open. This holds for uncountable families as well.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (0, 1-1/n) = (0,1)\) is open. Even though each interval misses the right endpoint, the union still does not include 1.
  • In \(\mathbb{R}\), \(\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty (-1/n, 1+1/n) = [0,1]\) is closed. The intersection includes the endpoints 0 and 1, which are not interior points.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: For a continuous function \(f\colon [a, b] \to \mathbb{R}\) and any \(\varepsilon > 0\text{,}\) there exists a polynomial \(P\colon [a, b]\to\mathbb{R}\) such that \(\|P-f\|_\infty < \varepsilon\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Any continuous function on a closed interval can be approximated as closely as desired by a polynomial.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text: • Polynomials are dense in \(C^0([a,b])\) with respect to the uniform norm.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
• Any polynomial can be "approximated" by itself accurately.
  • Continuous functions, e.g., \(f(x)=\mathrm e^x\), over the entirety of \(\mathbb{R}\) aren't always uniformly approximable by polynomials.

docs.title: Definition
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is defined as

$$ f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n x) $$ where \(0<a<1\) and \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text:
The Weierstrass function is one of the most famous examples of continuous but nowhere differentiable functions. In the original paper, this function is defined as \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty a^n \cos(b^n \pi x)\) where  \(0<a<1\text{,}\) \(b\) is a positive odd number, and \(ab>1+\dfrac{3\pi}{2}\text{.}\)

The Weierstrass function is based on the earlier Riemann function \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \dfrac{\sin(n^2 x)}{n^2}\text{,}\) which has also been called the Weierstrass function in some textbooks.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The Weierstrass function is continuous everywhere as long as \(0<a<1\text{.}\)
  • The Weierstrass function is nowhere differentiable if \(ab>1\text{.}\)

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is a particular Weierstrass function.

docs.title: Theorem
docs.text: Suppose \((f_n)_{n=1}^\infty\) is a sequence of bounded functions on \(X\) such that the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty \|f_n\|_\infty\) converges. Then, the series \(\displaystyle \sum_{n=1}^\infty f_n(x)\rightrightarrows f\text{.}\)

docs.title: Interpretation
docs.text: Since each function is uniformly small and their sizes add up to a finite number, the whole series converges uniformly.

docs.title: Key Results
docs.text:
• The limit function \(f\) is also bounded on \(X\).
  • Due to the uniform limit theorem, if each \(f_n\) is continuous, then the limit function \(f\) is continuous.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: • The series \(\displaystyle f(x) = \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x)\) is convergent due to the Weierstrass \(M\)-test: $$ \sum_{n=1}^\infty \left| \frac{1}{2^n} \cos(3^n x) \right| \leq \sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{1}{2^n} = 1. $$
